chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Washsha' from Aban ibn Uthman from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said:

I asked him about the man who swears to another man regarding food, telling him to eat, but he does not eat it. Is there expiation upon him for that? And what is the oath in which expiation is obligatory? He said: The expiation is for the one who swears regarding chattels that he will not sell them or buy them, then it becomes apparent to him [to do the opposite], so he expiates for his oath. And if he swears regarding something, and doing it is better than leaving it, let him do that which is better, and there is no expiation upon him. That is merely from the footsteps of Satan.
ai.seo_question: When does an oath require expiation in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between oaths of abstention, which require expiation upon breaking, and oaths of commission where the sworn act is inherently good, in which case one simply performs the act without expiation. This ruling highlights the principle of 'ease' in Shia jurisprudence, categorizing casual or minor oaths as 'footsteps of Satan' to encourage mindfulness without excessive burden. The hadith serves as a practical guide for daily conduct, emphasizing that the intent and nature of the oath determine the legal consequence.
